passages.title: A problem without borders
passages.text: Water scarcity is often seen as a problem for dry countries alone. In reality, it poses a threat to the economy and stability of entire regions. Not only does a lack of clean water damage public health, but it also forces farmers to abandon their land and move to cities that are already overcrowded. In some areas, millions of people have been displaced by droughts that lasted several years. The crisis we see in the headlines is just the tip of the iceberg. Behind it lie decades of poor planning, wasteful irrigation and unequal access to resources. Within the same country, wealthy neighborhoods may have swimming pools while poorer districts receive water for only a few hours a day. Tackling the problem requires cooperation across borders, since rivers rarely respect political boundaries. Campaigns to raise awareness have had some success, and new technologies have made it cheaper to recycle water. Yet without investment on a much larger scale, these efforts will remain a drop in the bucket. Only when governments treat water as a shared resource rather than a national possession will lasting solutions be found.

passages.title: Is the world getting better?
passages.text: Admittedly, the news rarely gives us reasons to be cheerful. Wars, natural disasters and economic crises dominate the headlines, and the number of people displaced by conflict has reached record levels. Even so, some researchers insist that, by many measures, the world is getting better. Over the last few decades, extreme poverty has fallen sharply, fewer children die before their fifth birthday and more girls than ever attend school. Whereas a century ago most adults could not read, today the vast majority can. Much as these figures deserve to be celebrated, they can also be misleading. Global averages hide enormous differences between and within countries, and inequality has grown in many places even as average incomes have risen. Progress, moreover, is not guaranteed: a single pandemic or a long war can undo years of improvement. Critics also point out that focusing on good news may make people complacent. Nevertheless, there is a strong argument for reporting progress as well as problems. People who believe that nothing ever changes are less likely to support the policies that have actually worked. Hope, in other words, is not naive; it is a precondition for action.

points: Inversión negativa: con «Never» o «Not only» al inicio, el auxiliar va antes del sujeto.
«Not only did the drought destroy crops, but it also…» suena formal y enfático.
Las colocaciones son combinaciones fijas: «pose a threat», «raise awareness», «tackle a problem».

mistake.wrong: Not only the drought destroyed crops, but it also forced thousands to leave.
mistake.right: Not only did the drought destroy crops, but it also forced thousands to leave.
mistake.note: Con «Not only» al inicio, invierte como en una pregunta: auxiliar + sujeto + verbo.

points: «Much as» + oración es por mucho que: «Much as I admire their work, I can't support it».
«Admittedly» reconoce un punto en contra antes de argumentar: hay que reconocer que…
«Even so» significa aun así: retomas tu postura después de esa concesión.
Son conectores de un argumento con matices, más formales que «but» o «although».

mistake.note: “Por mucho que” no se traduce palabra por palabra: usa «Much as» + sujeto + verbo.
